overview: The Haudenosaunee are a continuing alliance of Native nations whose heartlands include present-day New York. “Iroquois” is the imported map label. Its early outline extends far into New England and should not be mistaken for a precise boundary of the confederacy.

periods.title: Communities and the Great Peace
periods.summary: Member nations maintained their own identities while sharing political traditions of the Great Peace.

periods.title: War and colonial pressure
periods.summary: The American Revolutionary era brought destructive campaigns against Haudenosaunee communities.

items.text: Onondaga’s account of the Great Peace tells how the Peacemaker and Hiawatha helped bring formerly warring nations together. The longhouse became a political image: different nations could share responsibilities while retaining their own places within the alliance.

At Onondaga, clan membership passes through mothers. People of the same clan in another Haudenosaunee nation are also treated as relatives. That connection could make a journey feel less like arriving among strangers and more like visiting extended family.

Clan Mothers select the spokesmen who represent their clans in council. They also have authority to remove a leader after warnings if he fails his responsibilities. Leadership is a relationship with the community, not simply a powerful man’s personal possession.

The same account describes Clan Mothers naming babies and teaching younger and older people. Political responsibility, family life and education are closely connected. A child’s name belongs within a continuing community, with names available for later generations.

A traditional Onondaga longhouse held related families of a clan. A newly married husband moved into his wife’s family longhouse. Aunts and grandparents helped raise children, so home life extended beyond the parents and children of one small household.

At the Mohawk village of Garoga, archaeologists found thirteen longhouses within a palisade. Radiocarbon evidence places this settlement around 1550 to 1582. The remains give a particular village and period behind the general image of a Haudenosaunee longhouse.

Garoga also yielded thousands of pottery fragments and 43 lumps of unfired clay, probably prepared for making vessels. Pots with carefully shaped collars and incised patterns served cooking and storage. An unfinished lump can reveal the workshop behind a finished bowl.

Onondaga’s account of lacrosse describes handmade hickory sticks and teams formed by clans or by younger and older men. The game has ceremonial importance as well as athletic skill. Its meaning reaches beyond the score at the end.

Wampum beads require cutting, rounding, smoothing and drilling shell. Speakers use the woven strings and belts to remember agreements and histories. The Onondaga Nation describes them as living records whose meaning is carried through knowledgeable people and repeated telling.

An invitation to council could combine wampum with a notched wooden stick. Removing a notch each day counted down to the meeting. It was a calendar reminder with no battery to charge, carried together with the reason everyone needed to gather.

A modern written Onondaga sample is “Oñgwehoñwe’”, translated by the Nation as “the Real People”. Its language page connects the term with songs and identity. This is today’s Latin-script presentation; wampum itself is not an alphabet spelling out these words.

The 1779 American campaign burned villages and food supplies, causing displacement and hardship. Onondaga families later rebuilt in smaller houses while maintaining kinship and government. Their history continues beyond warfare and beyond the map’s 1783 endpoint.

ending.text: War and dispossession greatly reduced Haudenosaunee lands, but the confederacy and its nations did not end in 1783. Member communities continue their governments, languages and ceremonies; Onondaga maintains its council and longhouse on part of its ancestral territory.
